implementation_notes: Core Data's NSManagedObjectContext is the identity map: a single managed object instance exists in one and only one context, every fetched object registers with an NSManagedObjectID, and object(with:)/registeredObject(for:) return the registered instance instead of a second copy - the classic keyed map is replaced by context-scoped uniquing plus faults. Scope the context to the unit of work (view context for UI, private contexts for background work) and reset() or discard it at the end. SwiftData's ModelContext is the newer realization: registeredModel(for:) resolves a persistent identifier back to the registered model, but it requires Swift 5.9 / iOS 17+.
code_sketch:
let ctx = container.viewContext                    // one context = one identity map
let a = try ctx.fetch(customerRequest).first!
let b = ctx.registeredObject(for: a.objectID)      // same instance
precondition(a === b)
ctx.reset()                                        // drop the map at unit-of-work end
pitfalls: Uniqueness is per context, not global: two contexts hold two instances of the same row - merge with mergeChanges(fromRemoteContextSave:)/automaticallyMergesChangesFromParent instead of passing objects across contexts.
Managed objects and contexts are queue-confined: crossing threads requires perform/performAndWait or a new context, otherwise you get crashes and corrupted state.
Without retainsRegisteredObjects (default false) only strongly referenced objects stay registered, and reset() throws away pending changes - plan staleness and object lifetime explicitly.

variants.name: SwiftData ModelContext registry
variants.implementation_notes: SwiftData replaces Core Data's context with ModelContext: fetched models are registered with the context and registeredModel(for:) resolves a persistent identifier back to the registered instance, so the identity map is again context-scoped and implicit, while @Model macro declarations and the container/context lifecycle take the place of NSManagedObjectContext. Choose it for new Swift 5.9+/iOS 17+ apps; stay on Core Data below that floor or when you need its mature faulting and conflict-merge machinery.
pitfalls: ModelContext is not Sendable and is bound to its actor: passing model instances between contexts duplicates identity - re-fetch by persistent identifier instead.
SwiftData's identity and conflict handling are younger than Core Data's: verify uniquing behaviour for your fetch predicates and batch operations instead of assuming cross-context identity.
